A 15-year-old girl, 2 years after menarche, has a right thoracic curve with a Cobb angle of 55° and Risser grade 4. She is unhappy with her rib prominence and shoulder asymmetry. Neurological examination is normal.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Boston brace for 23 hours a day
mcq.e: Curves above about 50° tend to progress even after skeletal maturity and are cosmetically unacceptable, so surgery is indicated. Posterior segmental instrumentation with pedicle screws and rods corrects the curve through the mobile discs. Bracing works only in growing children with moderate curves.
w: Wrong - bracing does not control a 55° curve near maturity.
Wrong - curves over 50° keep progressing in adulthood.
Wrong - bracing is ineffective at this size and maturity.
Correct - curve over 50° with cosmetic concern: posterior fusion.
Wrong - hemivertebra excision is for congenital scoliosis.

mcq.stem:
A 12-year-old girl is referred after her teacher noticed she stands crookedly. Standing, there is a mild lumbar curve convex to the left. On forward bending the curve disappears and there is no rib or lumbar prominence. Leg lengths are equal and she has no back pain.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: A curve that disappears on forward bending, with no rotational prominence, is non-structural. With equal leg lengths and no pain, it is postural scoliosis, which usually does not progress. Structural curves, such as idiopathic ones, persist with a rib hump on Adams test.
w: Wrong - idiopathic scoliosis is structural with a hump on forward bending.
Wrong - compensatory curves need a leg length or pelvic cause.
Correct - disappears on forward bend, equal legs, no pain = postural.
Wrong - congenital curves are structural with vertebral anomalies.
Wrong - sciatic scoliosis is painful, from nerve root irritation.

mcq.stem:
A 10-year-old boy has a lumbar curve on standing examination. There is no rib hump on forward bending. His anterior superior iliac spines are at different heights and his right leg is 2.5 cm shorter after an old femoral fracture.
Which manoeuvre best confirms the cause of the curve?
o: Measure Cobb angle on a standing X-ray
Assess Risser grade on pelvic X-ray
mcq.e: Compensatory scoliosis results from pelvic tilt due to a short leg or hip disease. Sitting removes the effect of leg length, so the curve disappears when the child sits (or stands on a block). It resolves once the primary problem is corrected.
w: Wrong - Cobb angle measures size, not the cause.
Wrong - Risser grade assesses skeletal maturity.
Wrong - MRI is not needed for a clear compensatory cause.
Correct - the curve vanishes seated if leg length is the cause.
Wrong - bending films assess curve flexibility for surgery.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old boy has a curvature of the spine noted by his parents. There is a tuft of hair over the lower thoracic spine. Radiographs show a hemivertebra at T11 with a 25° curve.
Which additional investigation is most important to look for associated anomalies outside the spine?
mcq.e: Congenital scoliosis from failure of formation (hemivertebra) or segmentation (bar) is commonly associated with renal, cardiac and neurological anomalies, because these develop at the same embryological time. Renal ultrasound and echocardiography are needed, and MRI of the spine for dysraphism. Progressive congenital curves do not respond to bracing.
w: Wrong - bone density is not the concern in congenital scoliosis.
Wrong - CK screens for muscular dystrophy in neuromuscular curves.
Correct - renal anomalies are commonly associated with hemivertebra.
Wrong - nerve conduction studies do not screen for associated anomalies.
Wrong - a bone scan has no role here.

mcq.stem:
An 11-year-old girl with a right thoracic curve of 18° is reviewed in clinic. She has no back pain and normal neurology.
Which finding at this visit most increases her risk of curve progression?
o: Risser grade 5 on the pelvic radiograph
mcq.e: Progression is driven by remaining growth. Risser grades 0-2 indicate active growth and higher progression risk; 3-5 mean growth is slowing or complete. Premenarchal status also means the pubertal growth spurt is ahead. A fully correcting curve without rotation is non-structural.
w: Correct - much growth remaining = highest progression risk.
Wrong - Risser 5 means skeletal maturity and low risk.
Wrong - three years after menarche, growth is nearly complete.
Wrong - a curve that corrects is non-structural.
Wrong - no rotation suggests a postural curve that rarely progresses.

mcq.stem:
A 14-year-old boy with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy uses a wheelchair. He has a long C-shaped thoracolumbar curve of 50° with pelvic obliquity. He can no longer sit without propping himself on one arm and has an early sacral pressure sore.
What is the most appropriate first step in management?
o: Boston brace over 20 hours a day
mcq.e: Neuromuscular scoliosis typically forms a long C curve that stiffens and causes pelvic obliquity, sitting imbalance and pressure areas. Severe curves with loss of sitting balance are managed first with suitable seating support; if that fails, operative stabilisation is indicated. Treatment depends on functional disability.
w: Wrong - TLSO bracing is poorly tolerated and does not restore sitting balance.
Correct - seating support first; surgery if it fails.
Wrong - hemivertebra resection is for congenital scoliosis.
Wrong - loss of sitting balance and pressure sores need action.
Wrong - exercise does not alter a neuromuscular curve.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old man has 8 months of numb, clumsy hands with difficulty buttoning shirts and writing, and two recent falls from unsteadiness. There is wasting of the hand intrinsics, brisk reflexes in all four limbs, thumb flexion on flicking the middle finger nail, and upgoing plantars.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Loss of hand dexterity, gait imbalance and upper motor neurone signs (hyperreflexia, Hoffmann, Babinski) indicate cord compression: cervical myelopathy, commonly from spondylosis. Radiculopathy gives dermatomal arm pain and reduced reflexes at one level. MRI confirms; progressive myelopathy needs surgical decompression.
w: Wrong - carpal tunnel causes no UMN signs or gait disturbance.
Wrong - radiculopathy gives LMN signs (reduced reflexes) in one root.
Wrong - neuropathy reduces reflexes rather than making them brisk.
Wrong - lumbar stenosis cannot produce hand or UMN upper limb signs.
Correct - clumsy hands, falls and UMN signs = cord compression.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old woman has neck pain radiating to the lateral forearm and thumb, with numbness of the thumb and index finger. Elbow flexion and wrist extension are weak and the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are reduced. Extending and rotating her neck to the right with axial pressure reproduces the arm pain.
Which nerve root is most likely affected?
mcq.e: A positive Spurling's test with dermatomal pain and LMN signs indicates cervical radiculopathy. C6 supplies the thumb and index finger, elbow flexion and wrist extension, and the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes. C7 affects the middle finger and triceps reflex. Lecturer pearl.
w: Wrong - C5 affects the shoulder (deltoid) and lateral upper arm.
Wrong - C7 affects the middle finger, triceps and triceps reflex.
Wrong - C8 affects the little finger and finger flexors.
Wrong - T1 affects the medial arm and hand intrinsics.
Correct - thumb, wrist extension, biceps and brachioradialis reflex = C6.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man has a year of bilateral buttock and thigh heaviness after walking about 200 m. He has to sit down or lean forward on a shopping trolley for relief, but can cycle for 30 minutes without symptoms. Pedal pulses are palpable and ABPI is 1.0. Neurological examination at rest is normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Neurogenic claudication is relieved by sitting or flexing forward (the shopping-trolley sign), because flexion enlarges the canal; cycling in flexion is tolerated. Vascular claudication eases on simply standing still, is unaffected by posture, and comes with weak pulses and a low ABPI. Always check peripheral pulses.
w: Wrong - normal pulses and ABPI and relief with flexion exclude vascular claudication.
Correct - posture-dependent leg symptoms with normal pulses = neurogenic claudication.
Wrong - an acute disc gives sudden radicular pain, not walking-induced claudication.
Wrong - hip OA causes groin pain on movement, not relieved by leaning forward.
Wrong - neuropathy gives constant distal symptoms unrelated to walking.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old woman has neurogenic claudication limiting her walking to 100 m despite 6 months of analgesia and physiotherapy. Pedal pulses are normal. Surgery is being considered.
Which investigation is the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis and plan surgery?
mcq.e: MRI is the gold standard for lumbar spinal stenosis, showing the level and cause of compression (disc, facet hypertrophy, ligamentum flavum, slip). Plain radiographs show disc narrowing and osteophytes but not neural compression. Vascular tests are for excluding arterial claudication, which normal pulses already make unlikely.

A 60-year-old man has 6 months of worsening hand clumsiness and an unsteady gait. Examination shows hyperreflexia and a positive Hoffmann sign. MRI shows C5/6 disc-osteophyte compression of the cord with high T2 signal within the cord.
What is the most appropriate management?
mcq.e: Cervical myelopathy is usually progressive, and cord signal change indicates established damage, so surgical decompression is indicated to halt deterioration. Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion suits one- or two-level anterior compression; laminoplasty is used for multilevel disease. Conservative measures are for axial pain or mild radiculopathy.
w: Correct - progressive myelopathy with cord compression: decompress (ACDF).
Wrong - a collar does not stop progressive myelopathy.
Wrong - traction risks the compressed cord and does not decompress it.
Wrong - injections treat radicular pain, not myelopathy.
Wrong - manipulation is dangerous with cord compression.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old woman has mild neurogenic claudication and can walk about 800 m before needing to sit. She has no neurological deficit and no bladder symptoms. MRI shows moderate L4/5 spinal stenosis without instability.
What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Strict bed rest and lumbar corset
mcq.e: Mild stenosis without deficit is managed conservatively first: education, analgesia/NSAIDs, a non-impact exercise programme, aerobic fitness, activity modification and epidural steroid injection. Posterior decompression (with fusion only if unstable) is for failed conservative care or progressive disability.
w: Wrong - surgery is for failed conservative care or disabling symptoms.
Wrong - fusion is added only when there is instability.
Wrong - this is a surgical decompression technique, premature here.
Correct - conservative care first for mild stenosis.
Wrong - bed rest deconditions and is not recommended.
